prompt: A real account's summary prints `AccountMFAEnabled: 0` and `AccountAccessKeysPresent: 1`. What does it say?
hint: Both `Account…` lines are about one identity.

choices.text: No IAM user has MFA, and one of them has an access key
choices.why: The users have lines of their own (`MFADevices`, and the key count per user). These two describe the root user.

choices.text: The root user has no second factor and has an access key
choices.why: Right, and it is the worst pair an audit finds: the identity no policy restricts, reachable with a key that has no second factor. A real account wants 1 and 0.

choices.text: The console asks nobody for MFA, and the account's API needs one key
choices.why: MFA is set per identity, not for the console as a whole, and the API needs no key of root's to work.

choices.text: Nothing worth acting on: moto prints the same two numbers
choices.why: moto prints 0 and 0 because it has no root at all. In a real account, a key on root is a finding.

prompt: Which ARN names the root user of the account `123456789012`?
hint: The root user has no name of its own.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/root`
choices.why: That would be an IAM user somebody called `root`, an ordinary user with whatever policies it was given.

choices.text: `arn:aws:sts::123456789012:root`
choices.why: `sts` ARNs name sessions, such as `assumed-role/...`. The root user is an `iam` identity.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root`
choices.why: Right: the service, no region, the account, and `root` with no type before it.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/admin`
choices.why: An administrator user is still an IAM user, and an IAM policy limits it. The root user is not one of them.

prompt: The root password of one of the shop's member accounts may have leaked. Which control can stop that root user deleting buckets before the password is changed?
hint: Root is above every policy inside its own account.

choices.text: An IAM policy with an explicit `Deny`, attached to the root user
choices.why: No IAM policy can be attached to root, and none inside the account restricts it. That is what makes root root.

choices.text: A service control policy, set by the organisation from outside the account
choices.why: Right. An SCP limits every principal of a member account, root included; lesson 4 builds one.

choices.text: A permission boundary on the root user
choices.why: Boundaries are set on IAM users and roles. Root is neither, so there is nothing to set one on.

choices.text: Taking the root user out of the administrators group
choices.why: Root belongs to no group. Its permissions come from being root, not from a membership.

prompt: The id of an IAM user's long-term access key begins with the four letters ___.
hint: The transcript printed one beside `Active`.

prompt: Which of these are long-term credentials of an IAM user? Choose all that apply.
hint: Long-term means it lasts until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: A password made by `create-login-profile`
choices.why: Right. The login profile is the console password, and it stays until it is deleted or changed.

choices.text: The session token from `sts assume-role`
choices.why: That belongs to a role session and expires with it, an hour by default.

choices.text: An access key whose id begins `AKIA`
choices.why: Right. An `AKIA` key works until somebody deactivates or deletes it, which is why lesson 12 calls it the last resort.

choices.text: A token GitHub Actions gives a workflow
choices.why: That token belongs to GitHub's run, not to any IAM user, and it is good for minutes.

prompt: A new colleague at the shop will never have an IAM user. Can she still work in the shop's accounts?
hint: A principal is whatever signs the request.

choices.text: No: every request to AWS is signed with an IAM user's key
choices.why: Requests are signed by role sessions all the time, with `ASIA` keys no user owns.

choices.text: Only by signing in as the root user
choices.why: Root is kept for a short list of account tasks; daily work as root is the thing to avoid.

choices.text: Yes, through single sign-on, which ends in a role session
choices.why: Right. A person signs in at the identity provider and works through a role; lesson 11 sets it up.

choices.text: Yes, once she is added to the `developers` group
choices.why: A group holds users, and she has none to add. Membership gives permissions; it does not sign anything.

prompt: A trust policy names `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:group/developers` as its principal. moto stored it. What does AWS do with it?
hint: Is a group something that signs requests?

choices.text: Refuses the document, because a group is not a principal
choices.why: Right. A group never makes a request, so it cannot be trusted to make one. Each member gets permission to assume the role instead.

choices.text: Trusts every member of the group, now and in future
choices.why: That is what the author hoped for, and the reason the mistake is common. AWS refuses the document instead.

choices.text: Trusts the members the group had when the policy was saved
choices.why: No snapshot of members is taken. The document is refused before anything is stored.

choices.text: Accepts it, as moto did, since moto answers in AWS's format
choices.why: moto is more lenient than AWS here. Its format is AWS's; its checks are fewer.

prompt: Which of these is true of an IAM role?
hint: Think of what `create-access-key --user-name deployer` answered.

choices.text: It has an access key that AWS rotates every hour
choices.why: A role owns no key at all. Each session gets a new temporary one, which is a different thing from rotation.

choices.text: It has no credentials; each session gets temporary ones
choices.why: Right. Assuming the role returns an `ASIA` key, a secret and a token that expire together.

choices.text: It has a console password, set with `create-login-profile`
choices.why: A login profile belongs to a user. People reach the console as a role through sign-in, not through a role's password.

choices.text: It is a group of users with a trust policy added
choices.why: A group signs nothing and has no trust policy. A role is an identity of its own, worn for a session.

prompt: Match each prefix to what it identifies in AWS.
hint: Two are keys, two are identities.

prompt: The audit log says a bucket was deleted by `arn:aws:sts::123456789012:assumed-role/deployer/session1`. What does that tell you about who did it?
hint: Read the three parts after `assumed-role/`.

choices.text: An IAM user called `session1` deleted it
choices.why: `session1` is the session name the caller chose. A user's ARN is `iam`, with `user/` in it.

choices.text: The role acted by itself, with no caller behind it
choices.why: A role never acts alone; it has no credentials until somebody assumes it.

choices.text: Somebody who assumed `deployer`, under a name that identifies nobody
choices.why: Right. The session name is the caller's choice, and `session1` throws away the one clue the ARN carries. `bia-deploy` would have kept it.

choices.text: The root user, since the ARN belongs to `sts`
choices.why: `sts` is the service that issues sessions; every role session's ARN is an `sts` ARN.

prompt: bia's user is deleted by mistake and created again with the same name. A role's trust policy named her ARN, and now she is refused. Why?
hint: The ARN is the same; something else is not.

choices.text: The recreated user has a different ARN
choices.why: The ARN is built from the account and the name, and both are the same.

choices.text: It now points at the old user's unique id, not the new one
choices.why: Right. AWS turns the ARN into the old id when the user goes, so a new user with the old name inherits nothing. The policy has to be written again.

choices.text: New users wait a day before any trust applies to them
choices.why: There is no waiting period. The refusal comes from what the policy now names.

choices.text: Trust policies are cached per role session for 24 hours
choices.why: Nothing here is a cache. The trust policy itself changed when the user was deleted.

prompt: `create-role` printed `MaxSessionDuration: 3600`. How many minutes is the longest session the role gives by default?
hint: The number is in seconds.

prompt: Somebody writes the deployer's trust policy with the `aud` condition and leaves out `sub`. What has the role been opened to?
hint: Who else receives tokens from `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`?

choices.text: Nobody: without `sub` the condition fails and no token is accepted
choices.why: A condition that is not written is not checked. The policy accepts whatever matches the lines that are there.

choices.text: Every repository of the shop's own GitHub organisation
choices.why: Nothing in the policy mentions the shop's organisation; only `sub` would. Strangers' repositories match as well.

choices.text: Any workflow in any repository on GitHub
choices.why: Right. They all get tokens from the same issuer with the same audience, so `sub` is the line that names the shop's repository and branch.

choices.text: Only workflows that run on the `main` branch
choices.why: The branch is part of `sub`, which was left out. Every branch of every repository matches.

prompt: Why can `assume-role-with-web-identity` be sent with `--no-sign-request`?
hint: What does the GitHub workflow hold before the call?

choices.text: The token is the credential; the caller has no AWS key yet
choices.why: Right. The point of the call is to turn a provider's token into AWS credentials, so it cannot need AWS credentials first.

choices.text: moto ignores signatures, and AWS needs this flag too
choices.why: The call works unsigned against AWS for its own reason: the token proves who is asking.

choices.text: To keep the secret key out of GitHub's logs
choices.why: A signature never carries the secret. There is simply no key to sign with.

choices.text: STS is a global service, and global services take unsigned calls
choices.why: `AssumeRole` on the same service has to be signed. The difference is the call, not the service.

prompt: In this lesson, which of these did moto accept although AWS would refuse them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two refusals came from somewhere other than AWS's rules.

choices.text: A trust policy naming a group
choices.why: Right. AWS refuses it as malformed; moto stored it.

choices.text: A web identity token that was plainly made up
choices.why: Right. AWS checks the signature against the provider's keys; moto handed out a session.

choices.text: A SAML metadata document of 64 characters
choices.why: That one never reached moto: the command line refused it for being under 1000 characters.

choices.text: SAML metadata made of 1000 spaces
choices.why: Right. moto does not parse the document; AWS refuses one it cannot read.

choices.text: An access key for the role `deployer`
choices.why: moto refused that, as AWS would: `create-access-key` found no user called `deployer`.

prompt: Put the steps of a GitHub Actions deployment through OIDC in order.
hint: AWS checks the token before it reads the trust policy's conditions.
items: the workflow asks GitHub for a token
AWS checks the signature against GitHub's published keys
AWS checks `aud` and `sub` against the trust policy
the workflow signs its requests with the `ASIA` key until it expires
trap: Putting the conditions first is the common slip: a condition is only worth reading on a token whose signature is already known to be GitHub's.

prompt: The shop's company directory signs people in and exports an XML metadata document. Which kind of IAM provider does it become?
hint: One of the two standards speaks XML.

choices.text: An OIDC provider, the same kind GitHub's is
choices.why: OIDC carries JSON web tokens. An XML metadata document belongs to the other standard.

choices.text: A SAML provider
choices.why: Right. SAML 2.0 is the XML standard, and the role it reaches is assumed with `AssumeRoleWithSAML`.

choices.text: A group whose members are synchronised from the directory
choices.why: A group holds IAM users, and federation creates none. The directory stays the place people sign in.

choices.text: An IAM user per person, each with an access key
choices.why: That is the arrangement federation exists to avoid: long-term keys on AWS's side for people signed in elsewhere.

prompt: A partner's monitoring service runs in the partner's own AWS account and must read the shop's metrics. Which principal should the shop give it?
hint: The partner already has identities of its own, in another account.

choices.text: An IAM user in the shop's account, with an access key sent to the partner
choices.why: A long-term key in somebody else's hands is the arrangement lesson 12 calls the last resort, and here there is a better one.

choices.text: A role in the shop's account, with the partner's account in its trust policy
choices.why: Right. The partner signs in with its own identities and receives a temporary session; lesson 9 adds the external id that keeps the arrangement safe.

choices.text: Membership of the `developers` group for the partner's root user
choices.why: A group holds the shop's own IAM users, and nothing from another account can join one.

choices.text: An OIDC provider in the shop's account for the partner's AWS account
choices.why: An AWS account is not an OIDC issuer. Two AWS accounts trust each other through roles.

prompt: Match each need to the principal the lesson recommends for it.
hint: The table at the end of the federation section.

pairs.right: an OIDC provider and a role
single sign-on ending in a role session

pairs.left: a program with no other way in
pairs.right: an IAM user with a rotated access key

right_distractors: a group with a trust policy

prompt: A script on a laptop runs `aws sts get-caller-identity` and gets `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/caio`. What is it signing with?
hint: A role session would have answered with an `sts` ARN.

choices.text: caio's console password
choices.why: The command line never signs with a password. A password only opens the console.

choices.text: A session of a role that caio assumed
choices.why: A session answers with `arn:aws:sts::...:assumed-role/...`, not with `user/caio`.

choices.text: The credentials of the `data` group caio belongs to
choices.why: A group has no credentials; it would never appear as the caller.

choices.text: An access key of the IAM user caio, an `AKIA` one
choices.why: Right. A long-term key on a laptop: exactly the credential lessons 10 to 12 work to replace.

prompt: In this lesson moto handed a session of `deployer` to a caller the trust policy did not name. What should you conclude about the trust policy?
hint: What state was moto's checking in?

choices.text: That it is wrong, since AWS would have handed out the same session
choices.why: AWS would have refused the caller. The session says something about moto's settings, not about the policy.

choices.text: Nothing: moto's checking was off, so it judged no policy at all
choices.why: Right. With checking off moto lets every call through; lesson 9 repeats the call with checking on, and the trust policy refuses.

choices.text: That trust policies only apply to federated principals
choices.why: The trust policy applies to every principal that assumes the role, users and sessions included.

choices.text: That an `AWS` principal in a trust policy trusts the whole account
choices.why: It names one user here. Trusting the account is written differently, and lesson 9 shows it.
